title: Encode and Decode Strings
directAnswer: Don't join with a delimiter — any delimiter can appear inside the data. Use length-prefix framing: encode each string as `len(s) + '#' + s`. To decode, read digits up to the next `#` to get the length, then take exactly that many characters as the string. Because the length tells you precisely how far to jump, the `#` inside the data is never mistaken for a separator.

remember.formula:
encode: ''.join(str(len(s)) + '#' + s for s in strs)
decode:
  i = 0
  while i < len(s):
      j = s.index('#', i)
      length = int(s[i:j])
      word = s[j+1 : j+1+length]
      i = j + 1 + length
rules: Prefix each string with its **length and a separator** (`len#`) — the length, not the separator, decides where the string ends.
On decode, read digits until the **first `#`** to get the length, then consume **exactly that many** characters.
The separator `#` is only meaningful **in the length header**; inside the payload it's just data.
Handle the **empty string** naturally: `0#` encodes "" with no payload bytes.
Advance the cursor to **`j + 1 + length`** after each chunk — off-by-one here corrupts every following string.
whenToUse: Serialize a list of arbitrary strings into one string and recover it exactly
Data may contain ANY character, including your would-be delimiter
Designing a wire/file format where chunk boundaries must be unambiguous
Any 'pack many fields into one buffer, then split losslessly' task
antiSignals: Strings are guaranteed delimiter-free → a simple split on that char is fine
Fixed-width fields → pad to a known width instead of length-prefixing
Only one string → no framing needed at all
You control both ends with a typed format (JSON/protobuf) → use that library
remember.takeaway: Length-prefix framing is the bulletproof way to serialize variable-length data: by storing how long each chunk is, you never have to guess where it ends, so no character is ever 'special' in the payload. It's the same idea behind HTTP Content-Length, netstrings, and TCP framing — once you see it, every 'delimiter breaks on the data' bug disappears.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognise that any single-character (or even multi-character) delimiter is unsafe because the data can contain it, and reach for length-prefix framing instead. It's a serialization-correctness problem disguised as string manipulation.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Joining with a 'rare' delimiter like a comma or a non-printable char and assuming the input won't contain it — it can, and decode silently splits in the wrong place.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Name the length-prefix pattern, show it handles empty strings and embedded delimiters, decode by parsing the length then slicing exactly that many chars, and connect it to real protocols (HTTP Content-Length, netstrings).

problemStatement:
Design an algorithm to encode **a list of strings** to **a single string**. The encoded string is then sent over the network and is decoded back to the original list of strings.

Implement the `encode` and `decode` methods:

- `string encode(List<string> strs)` encodes a list of strings to a single string.
- `List<string> decode(string s)` decodes a single string back to the original list of strings.

You are not allowed to solve the problem using any serialization library functions (such as `eval`).
constraints: strs[i] contains any possible characters out of 256 valid ASCII characters
encode(decode(s)) must return the original list exactly (round-trip lossless)
understanding: Serialize a list of strings into ONE string so it can be perfectly reconstructed. The catch: each string may contain ANY character, so there is no character you can safely reserve as a separator. The fix is to record each string's length up front, so decode knows exactly how many characters to read and never has to interpret the payload.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the strings contain any character, including digits, '#', or newlines?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — all 256 ASCII characters are fair game. That's precisely why a plain delimiter fails and length-prefixing is required.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the list contain empty strings?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Length-prefix handles it for free: "" encodes as "0#" with zero payload characters.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the list itself be empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Possibly — encode returns "" and decode of "" returns an empty list. Worth confirming, though constraints here say length ≥ 1.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Am I allowed to use built-in serialization like JSON or eval?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — the prompt forbids serialization libraries. You must design the framing yourself, which is the whole point.

examples.explanation: Each string is prefixed by its length and a '#'. Decode reads 4 → "neet", 4 → "code", and so on.
The ':' is just a 1-char string — "1#:". No character is special in the payload.
First chunk: length 2, '#', then payload "#3" — the embedded '#' is read as data because we already know to take 2 chars. Second chunk "0#" is the empty string.

diagrams.title: Picking a safe framing scheme
diagrams.caption: The decision behind the encoding. A delimiter is only safe if the data can never contain it — which it can here. Length-prefix framing is the always-correct branch.

approaches.name: Single-Character Delimiter Join (Naive — breaks on the data)
approaches.whenToMention: Bring it up to expose the core trap, then show a concrete input that breaks it before moving to length-prefixing.

complexity.time: encode O(total chars), decode O(total chars)

hints: The simplest idea: join the strings with some separator character and split on it during decode.
Pick any separator — comma, space, even a 'rare' non-printable char. Now ask: what if a string in the list actually contains that character?
If the data can contain your separator, decode splits in the wrong place. With all 256 ASCII characters allowed, NO single character is safe.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Joining and splitting both touch every character once → O(total chars) time and space. The cost isn't the problem — correctness is.
approaches.explanation:
The instinctive first attempt is to glue the strings together with a separator, e.g. `",".join(strs)`, and `split(",")` to decode.

**Why it feels right.** It's a one-liner, it's fast, and it works on every test case you'd naively write — `["neet","code"]` round-trips cleanly through `"neet,code"`.

**Why it's fundamentally broken.** The decode step assumes the separator never appears inside a string. But the data may contain *any* of the 256 ASCII characters — including your separator. Encode `["a,b", "c"]` with a comma and you get `"a,b,c"`; decode splits into `["a", "b", "c"]` — three strings, not two. People reach for an 'exotic' delimiter like `\x00` or `"#:#"` to dodge this, but that only narrows the failure, it doesn't remove it: the prompt explicitly allows every character, so any chosen delimiter can occur in the payload.

**Why escaping is the wrong fix.** You *can* escape the delimiter (e.g. replace `#` with `\#` and `\` with `\\`), but now you've signed up for careful, bidirectional escape/unescape logic that's easy to get subtly wrong. Length-prefix framing sidesteps escaping entirely: by recording how long each string is, decode never has to interpret the payload at all.
approaches.insight: A delimiter scheme is only correct if the delimiter can never appear in the data — an assumption you almost never actually have. The robust alternative is to stop relying on a 'special' character and instead store the boundary information (the length) out-of-band in a header.

dryRun.intro: Watch decode mis-split because the comma inside "a,b" is indistinguishable from the separator.

steps.note: The embedded comma was treated as a separator — silent corruption

java.line: return String.join(",", strs); // unsafe: ',' may appear in the data
java.explanation: Glues with a comma — but a comma inside any string becomes indistinguishable from a boundary.

java.line: return Arrays.asList(s.split(",")); // mis-splits on embedded commas
java.explanation: split treats every comma as a separator, including the ones that were part of the data.

python.line: return ",".join(strs)  # unsafe: ',' may appear in the data
python.explanation: One-liner that breaks the moment a string contains a comma.

python.line: return s.split(",")  # mis-splits on embedded commas
python.explanation: No way to tell a data comma from a separator comma — silent wrong answer.

edgeCases.behavior: Join gives "," and split also struggles with trailing/empty fields — empty strings are another failure mode of naive delimiters.
Decodes to ["a", "b"] — proof that even a 'rare' delimiter fails when it appears in the payload.

pitfalls: Believing a 'rare' or non-printable delimiter is safe — the spec allows all 256 ASCII chars, so none is.
Trailing-delimiter ambiguity: "a," could mean ["a", ""] or ["a"] depending on split semantics.
Reaching for escaping to patch it — correct but fiddly; length-prefix avoids the whole problem.

approaches.name: Length-Prefix (Chunked) Encoding — len#str (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'prefix each string with its length so decode knows exactly how many characters to read'.

complexity.time: encode O(total chars), decode O(total chars)

hints: The problem with delimiters is not knowing where a string ends. What if you wrote down the length first?
Encode each string as length + a marker + the string itself, e.g. "4#neet". The marker only separates the length digits from the payload.
Decode: read digits up to the first '#' to get the length, then take exactly that many characters as the string — the embedded characters (even '#') are read as data, never as boundaries.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Encode appends a length header plus each string once → O(total chars). Decode scans left to right, reading each length then jumping exactly that many characters, touching every character a constant number of times → O(total chars). Extra space is the encoded buffer / output list, O(total chars).
approaches.explanation:
Frame each string with its length: write `len(s)`, a separator `#`, then `s` itself. The encoded form of `["neet","code"]` is `"4#neet4#code"`.

**Why the length makes the payload safe.** The breakthrough is that decode never has to *interpret* the string content. It reads the digits before the first `#` to learn the length `L`, then blindly consumes the next `L` characters as the string — whatever they are. If one of those `L` characters is itself a `#`, it doesn't matter, because we're counting characters, not scanning for a separator. The `#` is special *only* in the length header, and there it can't be confused with a digit. This is what the comma-join could never do.

**Why we need the `#` at all.** The length is a variable number of digits (`5`, `42`, `100`...), so we need to know where the digits stop and the payload begins. The `#` is that boundary. We can't be confused by a `#` in the data because by construction the parser is reading digits until the *first* `#`, and digits can't be `#`.

**Why the cursor math must be exact.** After reading a chunk that started at index `i` with its `#` at index `j`, the payload is `s[j+1 : j+1+L]` and the next chunk starts at `j + 1 + L`. An off-by-one here — say starting the next chunk at `j + L` — shifts every subsequent string and corrupts the whole decode. Walk this pointer arithmetic carefully.

**Why empty strings just work.** `""` has length 0, so it encodes as `"0#"` — a header with no payload. Decode reads `0`, consumes zero characters, and correctly produces `""`. No special case needed, which is a sign the design is right.
approaches.insight: Storing the length turns an ambiguous 'where does this end?' scan into an unambiguous 'jump exactly this far' move. That's the essence of length-prefix framing — the same trick HTTP uses with Content-Length and that netstrings and TCP use to delimit messages. Whenever a delimiter could collide with the data, prefix the length instead.

dryRun.intro: Read a length up to '#', then slice exactly that many characters; repeat from the new cursor.

steps.action: digits "4" up to '#' at j=1 → length 4
digits "4" up to '#' at j=7 → length 4
steps.note: Cursor lands exactly past the last chunk

java.explanation: Each chunk = length header + '#' separator + raw payload. The length is what makes decode unambiguous.
Scan digits until the first '#' — these digits are the length; a '#' in the payload is never reached here.
Parse the header digits into the exact number of payload characters to read.
Take exactly `length` characters after the '#' — embedded '#'/digits are read as data.
Advance past this chunk; off-by-one here corrupts every following string.

python.explanation: Build each chunk as len#payload — empty strings become "0#" automatically.
Find the header's '#' starting at the cursor; everything from i to j is the length.
Convert the digit run into the payload length.
Slice exactly `length` chars; no interpretation of the content needed.
Jump to the start of the next chunk — the precise pointer move that keeps decode aligned.

diagrams.title: Decoding "4#neet4#code" chunk by chunk
diagrams.caption: The cursor reads a length header, then jumps exactly that many characters. No character in the payload is ever 'special'.

edgeCases.behavior: Encodes to "2##30#". Decode reads length 2 → payload "#3" (the inner '#' is data), then length 0 → "". Proves embedded separators and empty strings both work.
Encodes to "0#"; decode reads length 0, slices zero chars → [""]. Empty string handled with no special case.

pitfalls: Off-by-one on the cursor (i = j + length instead of j + 1 + length) — shifts and corrupts all following chunks.
Searching for the length's end with anything other than 'first # after the cursor' — a later '#' in the payload must not be used.
Assuming the separator must be absent from the data — it can be present; only the header '#' is interpreted.

commonMistakes: Joining with a delimiter and assuming the data won't contain it — it can, so decode mis-splits.
Off-by-one in the decode cursor, shifting every subsequent string.
Special-casing empty strings instead of letting "0#" handle them naturally.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Trusting a 'safe' delimiter
commonMistakesDetailed.why: No single character is safe when the data may contain all 256 ASCII characters. Even an exotic separator can appear in the payload and break decode.
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
def encode(self, strs):
    return "".join(f"{len(s)}#{s}" for s in strs)  # length, not a delimiter, marks boundaries

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Off-by-one when advancing the cursor
commonMistakesDetailed.why: After reading the '#' at index j and a payload of length L, the next chunk starts at j+1+L. Using j+L (or j+1) leaves a stray character or eats one, corrupting every following string.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Scanning for the length's end incorrectly
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The length ends at the FIRST '#' after the cursor. If you scan for some other occurrence (or split on all '#'), a '#' inside the payload gets mistaken for the header boundary.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
j = s.rfind('#')        # WRONG — finds the last '#', not this chunk's header
length = int(s[i:j])
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
j = s.index('#', i)     # first '#' at/after the cursor is this chunk's header
length = int(s[i:j])

patternNote: Canonical length-prefix (chunked) framing. Recognise it whenever you must serialize variable-length data that could contain any character: store each chunk's length so boundaries are unambiguous. Same idea as HTTP Content-Length, netstrings, and binary-tree serialization with markers.
